books.section: Topic 6.10 Development of the Middle Class
Social Criticism in the Gilded Age
Industrialization, Corporate Consolidation, and the Gospel of Wealth

primary_sources: Andrew Carnegie, “Wealth,” North American Review, June 1889

stimulus.text:
“The problem of our age is the proper administration of wealth, so that the ties of brotherhood may still bind together the rich and poor in harmonious relationship.... The contrast between the palace of the millionaire and the cottage of the laborer with us to-day measures the change which has come with civilization. This change, however, is not to be deplored, but welcomed as highly beneficial.”

“The best means of benefiting the community is to place within its reach the ladders upon which the aspiring can rise — free libraries, parks, and means of recreation, by which men are helped in body and mind.... Thus is the problem of rich and poor to be solved. The laws of accumulation will be left free, the laws of distribution free. Individualism will continue, but the millionaire will be but a trustee for the poor.... Of such as these the public verdict will then be: ‘The man who dies thus rich dies disgraced.’”

(Andrew Carnegie, “Wealth,” North American Review, June 1889)
stimulus.source_note: Andrew Carnegie, “Wealth,” North American Review, June 1889. Public domain; wording checked against the 1889 issue (archive.org scan) and the Norton Voices of Freedom reprint.

stem: According to Carnegie, what is the best use of surplus wealth?

options.text: Hoarding it until death so it can be left as an inheritance
options.misconception: The passage praises the rich man who gives during his life, not one who waits until death.

options.text: Spending it on larger palaces for the rich
options.misconception: Palaces are the contrast Carnegie starts from, not the use he praises.

options.text: Placing libraries, parks, and means of recreation within reach of the public
Giving it to the government to spend
options.misconception: Carnegie wants the millionaire himself to administer wealth, not the government.

rationales.A: Carnegie says the rich man should attend to wealth during his life. Waiting until death is the use he rates lowest.
rationales.B: The palace is the starting picture of inequality. The praised use is giving to the public.
rationales.C: Carnegie names the best means directly: free libraries, parks, and means of recreation, the ladders upon which the aspiring can rise.
rationales.D: Carnegie leaves the laws of distribution free and makes the millionaire a trustee for the poor. The government is not the giver.
rationales.general:
Match the question to the sentence that answers it.
1. Find the sentence that begins “The best means of benefiting the community...”
2. It names libraries, parks, and means of recreation.
3. Those are the ladders upon which the aspiring can rise.
4. That is the use Carnegie calls best.
Remember: when a passage names the best means, quote its list, not your own.
